summary: Creates an IANA registry for IMAP keywords, the flags clients can set on messages, and defines how to register new ones. The goal is to help different IMAP clients interoperate by agreeing on what each keyword means. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a shared list of sticker names for emails, so every mail app means the same thing by a sticker called important.

questions: how to register an imap keyword
what does the imap forwarded keyword mean
what is the imap keywords registry
subtitle: A registry and a registration process for the flags IMAP clients put on email messages.

tldr.problem: IMAP keywords became de-facto standards in different ways, so clients sometimes used different names for the same meaning, or the same name for different meanings, which broke interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5788 creates an IANA registry for IMAP keywords with an Expert Review process, a registration template and a reserved '$' prefix for common-use keywords. It registers four initial keywords.
tldr.outcome: Keywords now have one documented meaning, owner and change procedure. The initial keywords are $MDNSent, $Forwarded, $SubmitPending and $Submitted.

facts.label: Common use means
facts.value: at least two independent client implementations

today: RFC 5788 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 8621 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Keyword Registry
sections.content:
IMAP keywords, from RFC 3501, are boolean named flags that clients use to annotate messages in an IMAP mailbox. They are an optional feature of IMAP, but the majority of IMAP servers can store arbitrary keywords.

Over the years, some keywords became de-facto standards. Sometimes different clients used different names with the same meaning, and some servers mapped them automatically. In other cases the same keyword was used with different meanings, which caused interoperability problems. RFC 5788 tries to prevent further incompatible uses by establishing an "IMAP Keywords" registry and allocating a special prefix for standardized keywords.
sections.eli5: Mail apps put little stickers on emails. Sometimes two apps used the same sticker name to mean different things, so a shared list was needed.

sections.title: How to Register a Keyword
sections.content:
A registrant fills in a template and submits it following the IANA instructions. The template asks for the keyword name, its purpose, whether it is PRIVATE, SHARED or BOTH on a server, whether it is advisory or may cause an automatic action, when and by whom it is set or cleared, related keywords and capabilities, security considerations, a published specification, a contact and the intended usage.

Registration requires Expert Review under RFC 5226. The request is posted to the Message Organization WG mailing list and IANA is copied. After at least two weeks for community input, the expert approves or disapproves it, and any refusal must come with a clear explanation. The expert should take no longer than six weeks to announce a decision or say more time is needed. Decisions can be appealed first to the Application Area Directors and then to the full IESG.
sections.eli5: To get a sticker name on the list, you fill in a form. A referee waits for people to comment, then says yes or no and explains any no.

sections.title: Common Use and Limited Use
sections.content:
There are two kinds of keyword. A keyword is for common use if it is reasonably expected to be implemented in at least two independent client implementations. Vendor- or organization-specific keywords are called limited use.

For limited use, the reviewer only checks that the name does not conflict with a registered name and is not too generic or misleading. The reviewer SHOULD refuse a registration if an already registered keyword serves the same purpose under a different name. For common use, the reviewer does those checks plus more: the keyword SHOULD start with the $ prefix, though this is only a SHOULD because some widely used keywords do not follow it. Common-use keywords SHOULD be standardized in IETF Review documents, and must be clearly documented and likely to ensure interoperability. If a keyword is already deployed, reviewers should favor registering it over demanding perfect documentation or a name change.

The reviewer MAY upgrade a limited-use request to common use, or ask that a common-use request be registered as limited use.
sections.eli5: Stickers meant for lots of apps get stricter checks than stickers made by one company, and the special sign '$' marks the shared ones.

sections.title: Comments and Change Control
sections.content:
Comments on a registered keyword go to both the owner and the review mailing list. After a reasonable attempt to contact the owner, a commenter may ask the expert to attach the comment to the registration itself.

The owner can request a change to a published registration, including a change to the intended usage field, by following the same procedure as the first registration. The contact and owner fields are the exception: the owner can change them by informing IANA, without discussion or review. The IESG may reassign responsibility for a keyword, for example when the owner has died or is out of contact.

Registrations MUST NOT be deleted. A keyword that is no longer appropriate can be declared DEPRECATED by changing its intended usage field. The IESG owns all common-use keywords published in an IETF Review document.
sections.eli5: Once a sticker is on the list it stays there forever. If it is no longer a good idea, it just gets a 'please do not use' label.

sections.title: The Four Initial Keywords
sections.content:
IANA registered four keywords, all with intended usage COMMON and the IESG as owner.

  • $MDNSent (SHARED) records that a Message Disposition Notification must not be sent for the message. A client sets it when it acts on an MDN request or uploads a sent or draft message, and a delivery agent can set it too. It SHOULD NOT be cleared once set. See RFC 3503.
  • $Forwarded (BOTH) says the message was resent to another address, embedded in or attached to a new message. It is advisory and typically shows a different icon. It SHOULD NOT be cleared, and the RFC notes there is no way to tell whether a message was forwarded more than once.
  • $SubmitPending (SHARED) marks a message as waiting to be submitted. A message with both this and $Submitted is being actively submitted.
  • $Submitted (SHARED) marks a message as being sent out. A client sets it when it starts sending.

The last three are specified in RFC 5550.
sections.eli5: The first four stickers on the list say: 'receipt handled', 'passed along', 'waiting to be sent' and 'being sent'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IMAP keywords are a base IMAP feature, and this document does not change their behavior, so it adds no new security issues. Each keyword may have its own security considerations, which are recorded in its registration template.

The initial registrations show an example: a server that implements $Forwarded, $SubmitPending or $Submitted as a shared keyword may disclose that a confidential message was forwarded, is scheduled to be sent or was sent.
sections.eli5: If everyone can see a sticker on your email, they can learn that you forwarded or sent it, even when the email was private.
